hints: Focus on changing only one concentration at a time while keeping the other constant, this is how orders are found.
Look at experiments 1, 4 and 5 where [Y] is fixed at 0.10 and [X] is doubled then quadrupled, what happens to the rate?
Now compare experiments 1, 2 and 3 where [X] is fixed and [Y] doubles, check if the rate doubles or quadruples to decide the link for Y.
walkthrough:
**Use the isolation method**

To find the effect of one reagent, keep the other constant. That way any change in rate must be due to the reagent you changed.

Rate rule:
$$\text{rate} \propto [\text{X}]^m [\text{Y}]^n$$

**Check the effect of X**

Compare experiments 1, 4 and 5. [Y] stays at $0.10 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ while [X] goes $0.10 \to 0.20 \to 0.40$.

Rate stays:
$$0.0001 \to 0.0001 \to 0.0001 \text{ mol dm}^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$$

**Check the effect of Y**

Compare experiments 1, 2 and 3. [X] stays at $0.10 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ while [Y] goes $0.10 \to 0.20 \to 0.40$.

Rate goes:
$$0.0001 \to 0.0004 \to 0.0016$$

**Deduce the orders**

X has no effect, so order in X is zero. Y doubling makes rate x4, so rate is proportional to $[\text{Y}]^2$, not to $[\text{Y}]$.

$$\text{rate} = k[\text{Y}]^2$$

options.A: Incorrect. Directly proportional would mean doubling [X] doubles rate. Experiments 1, 4 and 5 show [X] doubles and quadruples but rate stays at 0.0001, so X has no effect.
options.B: Incorrect. Rate does increase with [Y], but not directly proportionally (first order). Doubling [Y] from 0.10 to 0.20 makes rate go x4 from 0.0001 to 0.0004, showing second order in Y.
options.C: Correct. When [Y] is held constant, changing [X] by x2 and x4 leaves the initial rate unchanged. The reaction is zero order in X, so rate is not affected by [X].
options.D: Incorrect. Experiments 1 to 3 clearly show rate increases sharply when [Y] increases, so Y strongly affects the rate. This is the opposite of the data.
